_about: The steering note for the human reader. reader_framing is their own working view in close to their own words; only they change it (via inbox.md). Every sweep re-judges each verdict against the current evidence and rewrites the rest.
reader_framing: Inference is becoming load-aware and adaptive: the stack fits itself to what you have and to the traffic it sees. Agents tuning the stack, open and frontier models side by side, routing, speculative decoders and tuning for a domain are all parts of that one move, and I want to know how to build such a system.

verdicts.part: Load-aware, fitted to what you have
verdicts.short: Seven levers can move with the load, and four are in production somewhere.
verdicts.note: This is the frame the evidence supports best. Routing follows where the cache is, the cluster split follows the traffic mix, speculation follows the domain and the batch size, and kernels are regenerated per model and chip. One megakernel could not span two chips. The caution: almost all of it is measured on one workload class, coding agents, and one public trace set.

verdicts.short: They connect through the prompt cache and the model: change one lever and others must be redone.
verdicts.note: Yes, and the connections are concrete. A cache belongs to one model on one machine, so it fixes how often a model can be chosen and where a request must go. A drafter belongs to one exact model, so tuning or swapping the model means a new drafter and a re-tuned engine. Splitting prefill from decode left one provider drafting tokens that decode never used. That coupling is why re-tuning is constant, and why agents doing it cheaply matters. One of those ties is now under attack: three research systems translate a cache from one open model to another, so a switch need not mean a full re-read. Nothing has shipped, each loses a few points of accuracy, and none crosses a closed model's API.

verdicts.short: Worth 34 to 45% on decoding so far. Most gains are class-level and shared.
verdicts.note: Like for like, tuning a drafter to one customer's own traffic has been worth 34 to 45%, on different baselines. Modal's 20%, once counted here, came from tuning to the coding-agent class, and its recipe carried over to other models, not customers. Tuning the model itself does better on narrow jobs, but those tunes go stale. Most of the gain sits at the level of the workload class and lands in the shared open engines.

verdicts.short: Driven by bounded agent hillclimbs. Nothing has been shown to compound.
verdicts.note: Driven by coding agents running bounded hillclimbs inside harnesses that people built, with people setting the goal and approving what ships. The recursive part is true only weakly: a model serves the agents that tune its serving. Nobody has shown gains compounding, and the label already sits on a system with no self-improvement in it.

reframe: Inference optimisation is turning from hand-craft into search. Agents rewrite kernels and engine paths against replayed real traffic, so the thing being optimised shrinks from a model to what you actually have: this model, this traffic shape, this chip, this month. The scarce asset is not the agent but the rig that tells you whether a change is real.
ignore: KernelBench scores quoted without the verified protocol. The baseline was too easy.
Single-stream, batch-size-1 tokens-per-second records. Real, but they say little about serving many users.
Arguments over which engine is faster at default settings. One flag explained most of the largest gap.
Laptops against datacenters. You said hardware is not the point, so those arguments are retired.

read_next.why: The best single explanation of why measuring is harder than optimising. Read the sections on benchmarks lying and on their own ablations.
The strongest counter-argument, from people with nothing to sell. Read it before taking any vendor number at face value.
The whole loop laid out by the people who maintain vLLM, including the parts they say they cannot do yet.

position.label: Provider
position.text: You run inference for other people's workloads, across many model families. You are here to build, to find open ground, and to judge where the value will sit. You would build the measuring rig first.

implications.head: The rig is the asset, not the agent
implications.text: Evaluation is the hard part: replayed traffic, an engine that reloads candidates, gates that catch fake wins. The usual gate misses six of seven numerical bugs; public traces overstated one team's capacity by 1.7x.

implications.head: Many models multiply three of the seven levers
implications.text: Each model needs its own drafter, engine and cache. Open engines tune a new model in about two weeks, gaining up to 2.9x; your work pays in that window, on the models carrying traffic.

implications.head: A kernel lead lasts weeks, so lean on upstream
implications.text: Both open engines run the loop themselves and absorb fixes fast; a general engine came within 6% of a bespoke one. For the long tail of models, upstream is your tuning.

implications.head: Open models are your volume; defaults are the contest
implications.text: Open models carry most tokens and about a quarter of spend. On public tasks no shipped router has beaten the best single model, so the harness's default model decides which sessions reach you.
